title: First-day counts gave no clear M6.5 event probability gain after 122 shallow M7 to below 8 earthquakes in 2011-2024
abstract: We tested whether the first-day count of nearby M5.5+ earthquakes improved the probability estimate for a nearby M6.5+ event on days 2-30. We used a fixed global ComCat snapshot. We selected shallow M7 to below 8 centers with past-only isolation. Each annual model used only earlier completed targets. On 122 test centers in 2011-2024, with 13 later events, adding log count to magnitude and depth reduced mean Brier loss from 0.104106 to 0.098290. The relative reduction was 5.59%. Its conditional 95% two-year block interval was -0.15% to 11.11%. One-year, four-year and spatial intervals also crossed zero. Some planned threshold and penalty checks had positive intervals. Thus, this sample did not establish a clear primary gain. The result is a small retrospective benchmark, not a real-time forecast or evidence that early activity has no information. Revised event data, sparse targets, overlapping sequences and fixed model choices limit the test. Code, aggregate scores, resampling draws, source hashes, an independent audit and a figure are included. External event records remain outside the package.

display.caption: Annual Brier loss differences and planned checks. Positive values favor the first-day count model. Intervals use two-year blocks and hold fitted probabilities fixed.

citations.reason: The published binary nearby-event test motivated this different chronological probability test. The source records overlap. This is not independent confirmation.
